# How Self-Improvement Memory Boosts Continuous Recursive Self-Improvement in AI

The video summarizes an article by Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind and Penn State researchers on continuous recursive self-improvement: when the model or benchmark changes, the harness optimizer loses what he has learned. The proposal is the Self-Improvement Memory (SIM), a memory of the optimizer himself that keeps the reasoning, the predicted result and the observed of each edition.

Video by Maurício Yokoyama Issei, published on November 19, 2026 (5 min 31 s).
Watch: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i0bV36ade8s

_The video and the transcript are in Portuguese. The minutes between brackets, such as [04:12], point to the excerpt of the video._

## An AI that remembers its own past

The video analyzes an article by researchers from Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind and Penn State [00:00]. The central question: how do you give an AI system the ability to remember its own past, and how does that memory help build more robust autonomous systems [00:00]?

The analogy of the video is a worker who forgets why he made every adjustment in a project [00:20]. Whenever the environment changes, it starts from scratch and loses hours of reasoning [00:41]. That's the obstacle the article attacks.

## The problem of amnesia

The article deals with continuous recursive self-improvement (CRSI) [00:41]. In this scenario, an AI optimizer needs to continue evolving the harness, the set of tools and instructions that involves the model, even after the benchmark or the model itself changes [01:02]. Evolution cannot rule out the lessons already learned [01:02].

The example shows the size of the problem. An evolved harness in Claude Opus begins with 68.41 points when it is taken to the Gemini [01:24]. It is less than the 73.89 seed harness without optimization [01:44]. All progress achieved is lost in changing models.

## Autoimprovement Memory (SIM)

The proposed solution is Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) [02:05]. The memory stays in the optimiser of the harness, not in the model that solves the task. It begins to record past editions and their results, as a logbook of evolution itself [02:05].

The differential is what memory holds. SIM does not only save lines of code: it records the reasoning behind each edition, the context and the expected result [02:28]. Thus the system understands why the previous choices themselves [02:49].

## How Memory Works

The video describes a four-step cycle [02:49]:

1. Group the old editions by the recurring problem they tried to solve [02:49].
2. Keep the justifications, the predicted result against the observed and the context of the evaluation [03:10].
3. Make the two modules of the optimizer, which proposes editions and what you choose between them, read the memory [03:10].
4. Attach each new attempt, so the base grows as the optimization continues [03:10].

## Results

With equalized budgets and starting points, the SIM surpasses the continuation only with the harness and the continuation only with root causes [03:30]. The tests covered six scenarios between data sets and four Opus exchanges for Gemini in four domains [03:30]. One is the jump from Terminal-Bench 2.1 to Terminal-Bench 4 [03:52].

In programming, with ten independent executions, SIM improved nine out of ten continuations [03:52]. The average gain was 2.36 points [04:13]. It seems little, but the p value of 0.003 indicates that gain is not luck [04:34].

## What changes for autonomous agents

The video ends with a provocation. If it is already possible to cure the amnesia of optimizers, agents who accumulate their own lessons without interruption can evolve much faster [04:55]. For the video, it is a paradigm shift that is worth following closely [05:15].

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why an optimized harness for one model gets worse in another?

Because the optimizer does not keep the reason for each adjustment. In the example of the article, an evolved harness in Claude Opus begins with 68.41 points in Gemini, below 73.89 of the initial harness without optimization [01:24].

### What does Self-Improvement Memory keep?

For each issue, it keeps the reasoning, the predicted and observed results and the context of the evaluation, grouping the editions by the problem they tried to solve. The module you propose and what you choose read this memory [03:10].

## About the video

In this video, we explore the concept of **Continuous Recoursive Self-Improvement (CRSI)** and how to **Self-Improvement Memory (SIM)** solves one of the biggest challenges in the autonomous evolution of artificial intelligence systems.

Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind and Penn State researchers have investigated what happens when the Google Cloud AI optimizer *harness* needs to continue to evolve after changes in the policy model or evaluation benchmarks. In practical scenarios, a *harness* evolved does not always transfer directly — as seen when a refined configuration in Claude Opus obtained a lower initial score than the seed model when applied to Gemini. 

The proposed solution is: **Self-Improvement Memory (SIM)**: instead of just equipping the model that solves the task, the memory is integrated into the optimizer itself. *harness*. SIM catalogs and groups previous attempts for recurrent failures, storing the justifications, the predicted versus observed results and the evaluation context. Thus, both the proposing module and the selector can reuse past learning and avoid repetitions of errors.

---

📌 **Highlights of the Results:**
* **Consistent Performance:** SIM has overcome approaches that use only the *harness* or only root causes in six scenarios between data sets and four between models (including Opus migrations to Gemini and Terminal-Bench 2.1 to Terminal-Bench 4).
* **Statistically Significant Gains:** In paired programming tests over 10 independent executions, the SIM improved 9 out of 10 continuations, achieving an average gain of 2.36 points (*p* = 0,003).
